text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's Austrian newspapers:
- Austria is considering sending 100 aid workers and police to Albania as part of an EU team. If necessary, Vienna would also send 50-100 military as protection.
- Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger wants to cut eight percent off budgeted investment this year. That would hit the universities, according to the ministry for science.

- A debate about the ruling Social Democrats' relationship to the far-right Freedom Party has flared up again after local elections in the province of Carinthia. There the Social Democrats openly targeted the Freedom Party vote.
- Austria was off-line for two hours on Tuesday when internet providers went on strike.

- Austria is losing ground to its competitors in terms of efficiency. According to an annual study by Swiss IMD, Austria has slipped to 19th place in IMD's international rankings from 16th in 1995/96 and 11th in 1994/5.
- Tension around the future of Creditanstalt's regional banks. Bank Austria could try to become majority shareholder in Oberbank, BTV or BKS.
- Debate over EU defence policy splits the bloc as it celebrates its 40th birthday. One hundred Austrians may be on their way to Albania.
- Even parliament was barred access to the internet on Tuesday by a two-hour strike by providers.

- Families are paying 10 billion schillings too much in taxes, according to the responsible minister Environment Minister Martin Bartenstein. He said reform, due to take effect on January 1 1999, was a matter of tax justice.

- Oberbank, BTV and BKS, three regional banks that are closely allied to Creditanstalt, are working on a new ownership structure to prevent aggressive takeover. They want to ensure that 51 percent of shares are in "firm hands", according to Oberbank chief Hermann Bell.
- The number of Austrian dairies will be halved over the next five years, the industry says.
- Chancellor Viktor Klima favours a referendum before Austria joins NATO. A decision is not expected before 1998 at the earliest.
- Moody's is still watching Vienna City's triple A rating. Moody's announced it had put Vienna on its watch list in December.
- First Austrian sees a possible fusion with GiroCredit from 1998.
